[requirements v3, part 1 of 3]

# Meta harness requirements, version 3 (2026-11-04)

## Goal

One terminal-first interface through which the owner never again runs Claude Code, Codex, Copilot or another agent CLI directly. It orchestrates, delegates, exchanges messages between and controls those vendor harnesses on the owner's own subscriptions, shares one persistent memory, and survives terminal restarts like herdr. Example: analyze with Codex gpt-6.1-sol, design with Claude Code Opus 5.5, implement with Copilot kimi-k3.

## Verified facts (2026-11-04; rung 2 installed binary, 3 vendor docs, 6 third-party repo)

- Claude Code 2.1.318, unmodified binary: `-p --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --verbose`; `--resume`, `--session-id`, `--fork-session`; `--model`, `--effort`; `--mcp-config` with `--strict-mcp-config`; `--permission-prompt-tool mcp__server__tool` or `stdio` (stdin control_request); interrupt by SIGINT or stdin `interrupt` (idle-tested only); cost and usage in output; `rate_limit_event` documented, not observed. A pending approval does not survive a process restart. Under `--safe-mode` the reported permission mode was `auto`. Rung 2 and 3.
- Anthropic text: no third-party claude.ai login or plan routing "on behalf of their users"; no collecting, storing or intermediating Claude.ai credentials or session tokens; an end user may sign in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own subscription; "Advertised usage limits for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans assume ordinary, individual usage of Claude Code and the Agent SDK." Rung 3.
- Codex 0.166.0: `codex app-server` JSON-RPC (experimental): thread/resume, turn/interrupt, approval requests, approvalPolicy, model/list and per-turn model, rate limits and token usage, MCP per thread. Restoring a pending approval after a restart not established. OpenAI terms on third-party automation of a ChatGPT plan not established; auth doc points programmatic use to API keys. Rung 2 and 3.
- Copilot 1.0.105: `copilot --acp --stdio`; initialize reports loadSession true, MCP http and sse, session list and close, auth method copilot-login; cancel is the base `session/cancel` notification (honoured: not established); model change via `session/set_config_option` (not established); `kimi-k3` listed. GitHub terms: no automation clause beyond no "excessive automated bulk activity". Rung 2 and 3.
- herdr 0.9.5 (Apache-2.0): closing the client keeps processes alive; after processes die it restores the layout and resumes agents that reported a session reference. Whether a custom pane can report one programmatically: not established. Rung 3.
- T3 Code (MIT): reference for Codex app-server and Copilot ACP message shapes only; its own ChatGPT OAuth broker conflicts with R0. Rung 6.
- basicly ledger: one append-only shard per writer, merged by git union, plus a process lock; catalog projection to CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions.md exists. Rung 5.

## Decisions taken

D1 Drive only official vendor clients with the owner's own login, on the owner's machine, for the owner's own use.
D2 Transports: Codex app-server; Copilot ACP; Claude Code binary in stream-json print mode. T3 Code is a reference, not a dependency.
D3 Memory is the basicly ledger through the tracker kit, plus catalog projection.
D4 Engines talk through the meta harness as an MCP server; every verified engine supports MCP, so there is no file fallback in v1.

## Requirements for v1

R0 Legal. Each adapter cites the vendor text that permits its path, with the date checked; it does not ship without one. The meta harness never implements a vendor login and never collects, stores, forwards or brokers a vendor credential; first-run setup shows the vendor's own login command. It is for the owner's own use and is not offered to other users.

[requirements v3, part 2 of 3]

R1 Adapters. Contract: start, resume, send turn, stream events, answer approval, interrupt, choose model, report usage. Each declares its approval channel (native, prompt-tool, unsupported), its unsupported operations and its supported vendor version range, checked by a handshake at start and before each workflow. An unknown event or method is an error shown to the owner. A vendor binary outside the declared range is refused by name with the upgrade or pin command.

R2 Isolation. Each engine session runs inside a boundary the harness owns (separate OS user, container or bubblewrap) whose only writable root is its step worktree. It cannot read or write the ledger, the audit log, sibling worktrees, the meta harness state, or another vendor's credentials and binaries. An engine that cannot run this way is disabled by name. Engines are launched with a harness-generated, engine-read-only configuration that forces ask-or-deny, sets the permission mode explicitly, and refuses bypass flags; the adapter re-reads the effective mode before every turn.

R3 Workflow. The owner writes or edits a step list (engine, model, permission profile, inputs, outputs, file scope); a planner may draft it read-only within a stated cap, and engines and models the owner names are binding. A preflight at confirmation checks login, model availability, version range and isolation for every step and reports all failures at once with fix commands. Nothing runs before confirmation. Steps run one at a time in v1. Each step's status (planned, dispatched, completed, failed, interrupted) is written before dispatch; a rerun resumes at the first incomplete step; a workflow with a failed step never reports done.

R4 Context and artifacts. Each step receives the projected rules for its engine, the artifacts named as its inputs and nothing else. Artifacts are files in a per-workflow folder with a declared name and format, recorded in the ledger by the step that produced them.

R5 Memory. Memory writes go through the basicly tracker kit with the step id recorded; the kit's sharding and lock are the concurrency control. write_memory returns a committed record id only after a durable write, else an error. Engine writes are notes that are never projected as rules; a rule or catalog change is a proposal shown as a diff for owner approval. Secret scanning runs on every memory write, log line and stored transcript.

R6 Messaging. MCP tools delegate, ask, read_memory, write_memory, report, reachable only through the engine's own session channel. Inter-engine messages are untrusted data marked with their origin and never enter the receiver's rules. A delegated step runs with the overlap of caller and target permissions. ask has a depth limit, a timeout that returns timed-out, and a visible child session shown under its parent with engine and model.

R7 Approvals. Only the meta harness answers an approval, bound to a nonce, the action and the session; the first answer wins. An approval shows engine, step, delegation chain and diff; the owner may allow an action class for one step. A pending approval blocks only its session, raises a notification, and after a configured timeout is denied and the step marked blocked with a retry command. Approvals never carry over a restart; voided approvals are listed. Each privileged action and its approval is recorded in the ledger.

[requirements v3, part 3 of 3]

R8 Sessions and resumption. Engine processes run under herdr, or a harness supervisor if herdr cannot host them, so closing the interface stops nothing. The service starts with the owner's login session, or is started by the client, which says so (including WSL). After a host restart each session reopens at its last completed turn through the vendor's resume; a turn with unknown outcome is shown as interrupted, with the reason, the kept worktree diff and the choices rerun from last artifact, rerun clean, take over by hand, or abandon. It is never re-sent automatically.

R9 Interface. A chat line, slash commands and keys, with a help screen listing every command. One timeline with each line labelled by engine, model and step. Each session shows one state: running-tool, awaiting-approval, awaiting-reply, awaiting-quota, idle, stalled, interrupted, with the last event time; a missing heartbeat for N seconds turns it stalled with a reason. A since-last-seen summary on start. A review screen per workflow with artifacts, diff, verification result, cost per engine and approvals, offering accept with commit, rework a step, or discard. A take-over command opens the vendor client on the step's own session and reattaches it afterwards. Every error names the next command. The control server listens only on a user-only socket with peer checks; engines have no route to it.

R10 Usage. Each figure is marked vendor-reported, estimated or unknown. At a quota limit the step waits as awaiting-quota with the reset time or unknown and offers wait, switch model, switch engine, or stop; no automatic move in v1.

One terminal-first interface through which the owner never again runs Claude Code, Codex, Copilot or another agent CLI directly. ## Requirements for v1

R0 Legal. As v3, plus: no adapter is built before its citation exists.

R1 Adapters. As v3, plus: an unknown notification is logged and passed on; an unknown request that needs a reply is an error. A nightly contract test runs each adapter against the latest vendor release and reports a break before the owner meets it.

R2 Isolation. Each engine process runs in a bubblewrap boundary (rootless Podman as fallback) owned by the harness. Writable: its step worktree, the workflow artifact folder, and a private vendor home for that engine only (its CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, CODEX_HOME or COPILOT_HOME, seeded from the owner's home). Not visible: the ledger, harness state, audit records, sibling worktrees, other vendors' homes and binaries. The vendor's own command sandbox stays on inside it. Launch config is harness-generated and read-only to the engine, sets the permission mode explicitly, and refuses bypass flags by name; the effective mode is read back from the session init event. Preflight runs one unpaid login-status call per engine inside the boundary and a feature-parity check of the owner's MCP servers, skills and memory, and reports every lost feature.

R3 Workflow. As v3, with: planner cap 100,000 tokens or 15 minutes; "nothing runs" means no model turn before confirmation (preflight may start vendor processes). Steps run one at a time; an ask or delegate child session may run while its parent waits. Status values: planned, dispatched, completed, failed, blocked, interrupted.

R4 Context and artifacts. As v3, plus: user-level vendor files are copied into the private vendor home only when the owner lists them.

R5 Memory. As v3, with: durable means shard written with fsync and committed to git; a secret-scan hit refuses the write and names the field.

As v3, with: action class is a tool name plus a path pattern, such as Edit(src/**); approval timeout 30 minutes; notification by terminal bell and desktop notification where available; privileged action means any write, shell command or network call. During a take-over the owner answers in the vendor client and the harness records the answers afterwards.

R8 Sessions. Each engine runs in a herdr pane that reports its vendor resume command with report-agent-session. Closing the interface keeps processes; after a herdr or host restart each session reopens through its resume command at its last completed turn. 1. Done state: a command and the output it prints.
2. Gates for the touched files green; commit; push; CI on main green.

### basicly delivery overhaul: plan v3 (2026-11-07)

Priorities: (1) task success: fast, correct, sound, through review and release; (2) a tracker that never conflicts; (3) a tested design method with mockups. Every phase is poka-yoke: wrong use is refused by name with the correct command. Every step has a size, a revert unit (one commit or one flag) and a done state that is a command plus the output it prints.

Round-2 grades (3 new reviewers, lowest shown): coverage 7, order 4-7, poka-yoke 6, done states 5-6, speed 5-7, consumer risk 5-6, security 6-7, recovery 4-6, reuse 6-7, size 4-5. Round 3 runs as the first job of /hill-climb (0.3).

-1.2 Pre-commit runs ruff, ruff format, pyright on changed files (added: no hook runs them today), secret-scan, identity-guard, tracker-path-scan and internal-info-scan. Every other pre-commit hook becomes a required CI job in the same commit. Agent hooks keep only safety guards; telemetry moves off the hot path. Done: `time git commit` on a one-file change lists exactly those 7 hooks and real time under 10 s; a test asserts the CI job lists every moved hook id; a revert of the commit restores the old hook list.
-1.3 A branch commit needs no record id; the id is required on the PR and the merge. Done: a test commits on a branch with no id and is accepted, and a merge without one is refused by name.

#### Phase 0: orchestration and intake (first; small to medium)
0.1 /swarm skill (.basicly/core/skills/swarm/, reuses the reviewer agent and lens_review.py markers). It refuses a lens with no rubric by name. Done (`pytest tests/test_swarm_skill.py -q` passes named cases): `/swarm <artefact> --lenses a,b,c` starts one fresh agent per lens with a rubric, a reading list and a word cap; a lens with no report prints `not run`; every finding carries path:line or a command and its output, else the synthesis marks it unverified; the synthesis is a verdict table plus numbered decisions with one recommendation each; numbers, root causes and absence claims go through falsify-first by an agent other than their author.
0.2 /hill-climb skill, built on /swarm. Done: round 0 fixes the artefact and a property list; reviewers grade, the author never grades its own version; new lenses each round; stop at two rounds with no finding of medium severity or above, or when no property rises 1.0, cap 5; each round prints its grade table; decisions go to the owner after the climb.

Phase 3 must not raise wall time or steps for a tier-0 change; a check compares against this baseline.

#### Phase 1: CI speed and dead weight (small)
1.1 Consumer side of -1.2: install prints each moved hook and where it runs now, after one release of notice.
1.2 CI speed: per-PR runs Linux and affected tests; the three-platform pyright and the full suite run in the merge queue and on main. Done: per-PR quality-gates under 8 minutes.
1.3 Delete scripts with no code caller (about 1,300 lines, to be re-measured); done when `rg` for each deleted name across src, tests, .github and hooks returns 0 with one kept name as the positive control. Deprecate the loop, supervisor and factory commands now (warning names the replacement); removal follows 3.8.
1.4 Lefthook: keep our dispatcher, which has tool matchers; native `ai:` has none in v2.2.2. A recorded check re-tests the next lefthook release.

#### Phase 2: conflict-free tracker (large; before any parallel lanes; kit change that works with no engine)
2.1 Layout: one immutable file per event, named by the sha256 of its exact bytes, in a folder from the hash prefix: .basicly/ledger/events/ab/<hash>.json. No clock and no writer id in the path. The fold dedupes by event id (reuse ids.evidence_id and the existing fold dedupe), so the same logical event written twice with different timestamps counts once. Writes use O_EXCL; an existing file with the same bytes is success; temp files live under .git/, never in the ledger.
2.2 One layout resolver is the only reader; it checks that each file name equals the hash of its bytes and quarantines a mismatch; a gate refuses any other glob of .basicly/ledger. A ledger format version file; an older kit refuses a newer format by name and prints the upgrade command.
2.3 No commit on any branch, main included, modifies or deletes a tracked ledger file; only `basicly tracker pack` is exempt. The gate is a required CI check on the merge-base diff (local hooks are skipped by forge squash merges). `basicly rollback` and reverts exclude .basicly/ledger/. Packs are new immutable files that keep event ids; pack takes the queue lock, runs on a file-count threshold, and the fold dedupes across packs and loose files.
2.4 Proofs: two branches, two worktrees and a second clone each write; every merge order and an octopus merge with git merge-tree, with and without gitattributes (simulating a forge); pack while another branch appends; the same event on two branches folds once; concurrent writers in one checkout; a revert on main; two packs on two machines; read time for 100,000 events under 2 s on Linux and Windows as a pytest bound; the old layout still reproduces its conflict as the control.
2.5 Migration (its own phase-sized step): `basicly tracker migrate --dry-run` first; legacy logs stay readable and old-format appends on open branches are accepted and packed on main; fold equivalence (record count and field hash) before and after on the real ledger; an interrupted migration test; a tagged pre-migration commit as the rollback point; migrate refuses to finish while an open branch predates it and lists each branch by name; legacy files deleted only after that list is empty; the upgrade test (a v0.42 consumer fixture with an open branch) is a step here with a done command.

#### Phase 3: the delivery process (priority 1; three worktree lanes after Phase 2)
3.1 Verification: the agent shows output; a fresh-context two-axis review (standards and spec, never merged) before the PR, built on the existing reviewer agent and /swarm, not a new reviewer. Tier 0 gets one review, in CI only.
3.2 CI by skill and command: `basicly ci init --provider github` first; bitbucket-pipelines.yml, bamboo-specs/bamboo.yaml and GitLab as separate records; Jenkins, Azure DevOps and CircleCI listed for later. Generated files: permissions empty at the top, never pull_request_target, actions pinned by full SHA, no secrets for fork PRs; a check refuses a file that breaks any of these by name; never overwrites an existing file without --force; plain `basicly install` never writes CI files.
3.3 AI review and security review in CI: claude-code-action with the code-review plugin and the security review action, same-repo PRs only, key in a secret or OIDC; a check refuses secrets in any job a fork PR triggers; every finding answered before merge; no key means the job fails as not run, never green.
3.4 Risk tiers (extends classify.py; off by default for consumers; `[review] humans` sets how many people exist, so a solo maintainer's tier 2 becomes 1 with a logged note): paths, size and a sensitive-path list read from the base branch set none, one or two approvals; editing the list itself needs two people; unknown paths or a classifier error mean two; enforced through forge branch protection and CODEOWNERS with stale approvals dismissed; an agent or bot approval never counts.
3.5 Merge queue (extends merge.merge_queue and `basicly worktree merge-queue`; designed before the pack step is frozen): provider auto, github, bitbucket or basicly, read at landing time; `auto` refuses to land when it finds no queue until `basicly` is set explicitly; the basicly queue refuses while a forge queue is on, and an unreachable forge API or a missing token counts as on (refuse); the proof that checks ran is a required CI status on the exact tree SHA, never local output; it lands with --ff-only only after checks ran on the exact tree; across machines it holds a lock ref on origin by compare-and-swap, as a lease with owner and expiry, with `basicly queue unlock --reason`; with no branch protection it says it is advisory.
3.6 Feature flags (native, no new dependency): `basicly flag add <name> --owner --expires --removal <id>` writes a flag registry; code reads flags through one small module with an OpenFeature-shaped interface; a missing flag or a provider failure means off and a log line; security flags cannot be overridden by environment; a CI gate fails on an expired flag or a flag with no removal record; a skill teaches release and deploy behind a flag.
3.7 Release and recovery (extends release.py; after 3.6): staged channels; a fix-forward-or-roll-back skill with a decision rule; `basicly rollback` turns a flag off or reverts a release through the same queue, with an emergency path behind an explicit flag and a logged reason; a rollback drill runs in CI on each minor release.
3.8 Retire what the new process replaces: the loop phases, the verify and validate gates and the reviewer and validator agents that it supersedes, each deprecated for one release with a warning naming its replacement.
3.9 End-to-end proof: one consumer repo runs PR, review, approval, queue, release, flag-off and rollback, recorded as a transcript.

#### Phase 4: solution design (medium; reuses the designer agent and validate-as-consumer)
4.1 design skill: grill the user (numbered questions, each with a recommended answer), then a design doc: problem, critical user journeys, options with failure modes, Zero-Decision implementation plan, agreed test seams, tickets sized to one fresh context.
4.2 UI: text wireframes, then an HTML mock rendered and screenshotted at every claimed viewport, judged against the journeys.
4.3 Review by /hill-climb with rubric lenses: zoom-out, implementation readiness, UX.
4.4 Tested: run the method on three sample tasks against a plain-agent baseline and record rework, findings and time.

#### Phase 5: cut and rewrite (large; one record per deleted check)
5.1 A check is deleted only when the gate-failure history shows no failure on main in the last 60 days and no regression test cites it; the deleting commit cites that history. Useful scripts are rewritten, not kept as they are.
5.2 Skills: user-phrase triggers, under 500 words, positive instructions, a suggested-skills handover; always-on files under 600 words; a wording gate refuses a term defined two ways across skills and always-on files, and trigger evals catch a skill that fires on the wrong phrase.
5.3 Engine removals already planned under basicly-gtb19bg.30.

#### Cross-cutting
- Every done state is a command plus its expected output; phases without one are not started.
- Every claim from a swarm carries path:line or a command; the author never grades its own work.
- Upgrade test: install over a v0.42 consumer fixture with an open branch before every release that changes a consumer.
- basicly's own changes ship behind flags where they change consumer behaviour.
- Dependency graph: -1 first; 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, then 0.4 and 0.5; 1 next; 2 before parallel lanes; 3 and 4 in parallel worktrees (3 owns src/basicly/merge.py, release.py, classify.py and CI templates; 4 owns skills and agents); 3.6 before 3.7; 5.2 after 0 and 4.
- Release after each phase that changes what a consumer sees.
